jabber.e: From Middle English jaberen, javeren, chaveren (“to chatter, babble”), dissimilated forms of jablen, chavelen (“to jabber”), from Middle English chavel ("jaw".
jabber.x: “What are you jabbering about, shipmate?” said I.

jackal.e: Borrowed from French chacal, chacale, checale, schakal, ciacale, from Turkish çakal, from Ottoman Turkish چقال (çakâl), from Classical Persian شغال (šaġāl), borrowed from…

jackass.e: From the phonetic similarity of "jack, ace" to "jackass".
jackass.x: Bobby, only jackasses go around saying how much money they make.

jackfruit.e: From jack (“jackfruit”), from Portuguese jaca (“jackfruit”), from Malayalam ചക്ക (cakka) / Tamil சக்கை (cakkai), + fruit.
jackfruit.x: Some fun meatless recipes include jackfruit sandwiches in place of pulled pork; black bean meatless balls or eggplant and shiitake “meatballs.”

jackhammer.x: A new skiercross pro tour is on the docket, as well as freeskiing. Just like racing, both require strong but supple legs rather than jackhammer quads.

jacuzzi.e: Genericized trademark of the proprietary name Jacuzzi.
jacuzzi.x: And, by the way, my Jacuzzi days are long gone.

jaded.e: From jade (“worn-out horse”), possibly from Old Norse jalda (“mare”). Jade as a term of abuse for a woman dates from 1560.

jaggery.e: PIE word *ḱorkeh₂ Borrowed from Indo-Portuguese jágara, jagra, from Malayalam ചക്കര (cakkara, “jaggery”) or Tamil சக்கரை (cakkarai), from Sanskrit शर्करा (śarkarā…

jaguar.e: From Portuguese jaguar, from Old Tupi îagûara.

jailer.e: Inherited from Middle English gayoler, gayler, jayler, from Old French jaiolier, gaiolier, from jaiole. By surface analysis, jail + -er.

jalebi.e: From Hindustani जलेबी / جلیبی (jalebī). Doublet of zalabiya.
jalebi.x: On the way he saw a sweetmeat seller making jalebis (spiral sweet). He was tempted. In his mind he thought he'd have some jalebis.

jalopy.e: Unknown. Perhaps from Jalapa, Mexico (now Xalapa), to whose scrapyards used cars were often sent from New Orleans starting in the 1920s.
jalopy.x: There's only a rough track and I doubt if that jalopy of yours will make it.

jamboree.e: Unknown 19th-century American slang. Chosen by Baden-Powell in 1919 for use in the Scout Movement.

jargon.e: From Middle English jargoun, jargon, from Old French jargon, a variant of gargon, gargun (“chatter; talk; language”).
jargon.x: He used technical jargon but I managed to catch the drift of his argument.

jasper.e: From Middle English jasper, jaspre, from Old French jaspre, a variant of jaspe (modern French jaspe), from Latin iaspis, from Ancient Greek ἴασπις (íaspis).

jaundice.e: From Middle English jaundis, jaunis, from Middle French jaunisse, from jaune (“yellow”) + -isse (“-ness”).
jaundice.x: But look in this new mirror, lovely friend. / Both gods and fairies wait on lovers' wills. / That jaundices be changed to daffodils!

javelin.e: From Middle English chafeveleyn, gavelong, from Old French javelline, diminutive of javelot, diminutive of *javel, from Vulgar Latin *gabalus, from Gaulish gabulum…
javelin.x: Flies the javelin swifter to its mark, / Launched by the vigour of a Roman arm?

jawbone.e: From Middle English jawe bone, a partial calque of earlier Middle English chawlbone, chawylbon, chavylbone, chawle boon, chavyl bon (“jaw bone”, literally “chavel bone”)…

jealousy.x: Jealousy was, however, aroused among the English nobility at the favouritism shown the Dutch newcomer.

jeans.e: From Gene(s) (also spelled Jean(s)), an obsolete English name for the Italian city of Genoa. Compare French Gênes.
jeans.x: Traditionally most jeans are dyed dark blue.

jejunum.e: Borrowed from Latin iēiūnum, neuter of iēiūnus.

jelly.x: Sam floored him perpetually, and beat his face to a jelly, without getting a scratch.

jellyfish.x: There are asexual variants among all sorts of creatures, including jellyfish, dandelions, lichens and lizards.

jeopardize.x: After having an affair with a junior, her chances of promotion were seriously jeopardized.

jeopardy.e: From Middle English jupartie, jeupartie (“even chance”), from Anglo-Norman giu parti and Middle French jeu parti (“a divided game, i.e.
jeopardy.x: The poor condition of the vehicle put its occupants in constant jeopardy.

jerrycan.e: From Jerry (“a German”) + can, from its use by German troops in World War II.
jerrycan.x: Anyone with half a brain and a jerrycan of fertilizer's got an army.

jester.e: From Middle English gestour; equivalent to jest + -er.

jetty.e: The noun is derived from Late Middle English gete, jette, jetti (“projecting upper storey of a building, overhang.
jetty.x: The boathouse was a stone one, with a narrow quay along each wall inside, and a small jetty sticking out beyond it into the lake.

jewel.e: From Middle English juel, jewel, juwel, jeuel, jowel, from Anglo-Norman juel, from Old French jouel, joel, joïel, hence French joyau, of uncertain origin.
jewel.x: Iachimo: 'Tis plate of rare device, and jewels / Of rich and exquisite form, their values great.

jeweler.e: From Middle English jueler, from Anglo-Norman jueler, or Old French juelier. By surface analysis, jewel + -er.

jewellery.e: Inherited from Middle English juelrye, from Old French juelerye, equivalent to jewel + -ery.
jewellery.x: The jewellery was very expensive in that shop.

jicama.e: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish jícama, from Classical Nahuatl xīcama, apocopic form of xīcamatl.

jiffy.e: Origin unknown; said to have been thieves’ cant for “lightning”. Also formerly written "giffy", to which a connection with gliff has been proposed.

jihad.x: The Jabhat al-Nusra media, with songs about jihad and martyrdom, is extremely influential.

jihadist.x: Like Muslim jihadists, Christian jihadists such as these two are willing to sacrifice as they seek to impose their religious tyranny on others.

jingle.e: The verb, which is older than the noun, is from Middle English gyngle. Onomatopoeic; compare jangle.
jingle.x: He heard the jingle of her keys in the door and turned off the screen.

jobseeker.x: It has taken people off the dole queue, and its online jobseekers board is updated daily.

jockey.x: They were jockeying for position toward the end of the race.

jockstrap.e: Compound of (dated slang) jock (“penis”) + strap; from the earlier forms bike jockey strap and jockey strap.
jockstrap.x: There are many accounts of men, back in the 1970s, work out in nothing but a jockstrap.

jocular.e: From Latin iocularis, from ioculus (“a little jest”), diminutive of iocus (“a jest”).
jocular.x: All we had was a short and jocular conversation.

jogging.x: His jogging of my memory helped me recall what happened that day.

joiner.e: From Middle English joynour (“maker of furniture, small boxes, etc.”), from Old French joigneor (“joiner, carpenter”), agent noun from joindre (“to join”), equivalent to…
joiner.x: I am not a joiner. I am reluctant to sign up as a member of any organization, because I generally can't find myself or my ideas in it.

jointly.x: They jointly raised the child, even though they were no longer married.

joist.e: From Old French giste, feminine of gist, the past participle of gesir (“to lie down”).
joist.x: Once the floor joists were in position, the framing of the next storey could continue, with a bressummer laid along their ends.

joker.x: Some joker keeps throwing eggs at my windows.

jostle.e: Originally justle (“to have sex with”), formed from Middle English jousten, from the Old French joster (“to joust”), from Latin iuxtā (“next to”), from iungō (“join…
jostle.x: Axia and Amory, acquaintances of an hour, jostled behind a waiter to a table at a point of vantage; there they took seats and watched.

journal.e: From Middle English journal, from Anglo-Norman jurnal (“daily”), from Old French jornel (“day”) (whence modern French journal), from Latin diurnālis, from diurnus (“of…
journal.x: The university's biology department subscribes to half a dozen academic journals.

journalistic.e: From journal + -istic (“adjective”). Also parsed directly as journalist + -ic (“adjective”), also used in sense of related journalism (having to do with journalism).
journalistic.x: This gang-bang speaks more to journalistic groupthink than to any real moral or legal reasoning.

journeyman.e: From Middle English jorneman; from journe (from Old French jornee (“a day's work, a journey”)) and mon; equivalent to journey + -man.
journeyman.x: Everyone must follow safety guidelines whether you're an apprentice, journeyman, or even master electrician.

jovial.e: First attested in 1590; borrowed from Middle French jovial (“under the influence of Jupiter; of Jove.
jovial.x: A long, jovial, inane laugh broke the sudden silence which had fallen over everyone.

joyful.x: The children were joyful on the first day of summer break.

joyous.e: From Middle English joyous, joious, from Old French joieus, from joie + -eus.

jubilee.e: From Late Middle English jubile [and other forms], from Middle French jubile, from Old French jubilee, jubileus (modern French jubilé), from Late Latin iūbilaeus…
jubilee.x: Was it for Peveril of the Peak, in the jubilee of his spirits, to consider how his wife was to find beef and mutton to feast his neighbours?

judicious.e: From French judicieux, ultimately derived from Latin iudico. Related to judge, judicial.

juggernaut.e: Borrowed in the 17th century into British English in India, either through Hindustani جَگَنَّاتھ (jagannāth) / जगन्नाथ (jagannāth) or directly from Odia ଜଗନ୍ନାଥ…

juggle.e: From Middle English jogelen, partly a back-formation of Middle English jogeler (“juggler”), and partly a borrowing from Old French jogler, jongler (“to have fun with…
juggle.x: He juggled home, school, and work for two years.

juggler.e: From Middle English jogeler, jogelour, iogular, partly continuing Old English ġeogolere (“juggler; magician.
juggler.x: Only when a juggler misses catching his ball does he appeal to me.

juggling.e: From Middle English jogelyng, juglynge, equivalent to juggle + -ing.

jugular.e: Late 16th century borrowing from Late Latin jugulāris, from jugulum (“the collarbone; the hollow part of the neck above the collarbone.

juicer.x: A keen juicer, she has tried all kinds of fruits and vegetables.

juicy.e: From Middle English jousy, jowsy (“drunken”, literally “full of juice (liquor)”). By surface analysis, juic(e) + -y.
juicy.x: I do not keep up with all the latest juicy rumors.

jujube.e: From Middle English jujube, from Medieval Latin jujuba or Old French jujube, perhaps via Old Occitan from Classical Latin zīzyphum, zīzyphus, from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον…

jukebox.e: First use appears c. 1939, from juke (“roadside café”) + box, replacing older collocational terms such as nickel-in-a-slot phonograph, coin-in-the-slot phonograph, and…
jukebox.x: "I love rock 'n roll So put another dime in the jukebox, baby I love rock 'n roll So come and take your time and dance with me"

jumble.e: From Middle English jumbelen, alteration of jumbren, jombren, a variant of jumpren, frequentative of jumpen (“to jump”), equal to jump + -le.
jumble.x: Why dost thou blend and jumble such inconsistencies together?

jumper.e: From the term jump (“short coat”) + -er, originally in sailors' jargon, ultimately of uncertain origin.
jumper.x: Significantly more cervical spine injuries were seen in fallers as opposed to jumpers.

jumpsuit.e: From jump + suit, referring to parachute jumps.

junction.e: From Latin iūnctiō (“union, joining, uniting”), from iungō (“join, attach together”). Equivalent to join + -tion.
junction.x: Their collaboration formed a fruitful junction of ideas.

juncture.e: Inherited from Middle English juncture, from Latin iūnctūra. Doublet of jointure.
juncture.x: We're at a crucial juncture in our relationship.

juniper.e: From Late Middle English junyper, juniperus, from Latin iūniperus (“juniper-tree”).
juniper.x: On the mountains a few junipers and piñons are found, and cactuses, agave, and yuccas, low, fleshy plants with bayonets and thorns.

junta.e: Borrowed from Spanish junta (literally "a thing gathered or joined"), feminine form of junto, from Latin iunctus, perfect passive participle of iungō (“join”).

jurisdiction.x: The case falls outside the court’s jurisdiction.

jurist.x: The distinguished jurist wrote extensively on constitutional law.

juror.e: From Middle English jurour, jurrour, borrowed from Anglo-Norman jurour and Old French jureor, from the verb jurer (“to swear”), or possibly from Latin iūrātor, iūrātōrem…

justifiable.e: From Middle French justifiable. By surface analysis, justify + -able.

justification.e: From Middle English justificacioun, justification, from Middle French justification, from Late Latin iustificationem, justificationem < iustificatio, from iustifico, from…

justify.e: From Middle English justifien, from Old French justifier, from Late Latin justificare (“make just”), from Latin justus, iustus (“just”) + ficare (“make”), from facere…
justify.x: How can you justify spending so much money on clothes?

justly.x: His valor, wisdom, and justice made him justly popular, but caused him to be regarded with suspicion at Rome.

juxtapose.e: Borrowed from French juxtaposer, corresponding to juxta- + pose, derived from Latin iuxtā (“near, next to”) + pōnō (“place”).
juxtapose.x: The artist used contrasting colors to juxtapose light and dark.

juxtaposition.e: Borrowed from French juxtaposition, from Latin iuxtā (“near”) (from Latin iungō (“to join”)) + French position (“position”) (from Latin pōnō (“to place”)).
juxtaposition.x: Using juxtaposition for multiplication saves space when writing longer expressions. a#92;timesb collapses to ab.
